description: Grammar game rule taxonomy. Six game sections, each broken into rules tagged with California Common Core (CA CCSS) Language standards, grade level, and how strict the rule is.
source_standards: California Common Core State Standards: English Language Arts & Literacy (CDE, modified March 2013), Language strand standards 1-3.

conventions.standard_codes: Strand.Grade.Number+letter, e.g. L.4.2c. High school bands written with a hyphen (L.9-10.2a) instead of the PDF's en dash. 'custom' = taught in the game but not named in any standard.
conventions.grade_min: Grade where the standard first introduces the rule (0 = kindergarten). For 'custom' rules this is the team's suggested grade. Adjust freely for the game's audience.

strictness.required: One correct answer; anything else is an error.
strictness.preferred: Standard usage, but the alternative is not wrong in all contexts. Flag gently; don't mark as an error in correction tasks.
strictness.style_dependent: Correct answer depends on the style guide or dialect. Store all accepted answers; never 'correct' one valid style into another.

conventions.italics_markup: Italics are written as *Title* (Markdown) everywhere in training data and the game UI.
conventions.default_style: us_general (American punctuation; serial comma accepted but not required).

sections.name: Capitalization
sections.description: Sentence starts, the pronoun I, proper nouns, and titles.

sections.name: Commas
sections.description: Lists, joining and separating ideas, complex sentences, and when NOT to use a comma.

sections.name: Quotation
sections.description: Dialogue, quoting texts, titles (quotation marks vs. italics), and special phrases.

sections.name: Sentence Boundaries & Ending Punctuation
sections.description: Periods, question marks, exclamation marks, and fixing run-ons, comma splices, and fragments.

sections.name: Connectors
sections.description: Parentheses, dashes, semicolons, colons, ellipses, and hyphens.

sections.name: Apostrophes
sections.description: Contractions, singular and plural possessives, commonly confused words, and plural letters and numbers.

rules.rule: Capitalize the first word of every sentence.
rules.correct_example: The bus was late again.
rules.incorrect_example: the bus was late again.

rules.rule: Always capitalize the pronoun I, wherever it appears in a sentence.
rules.correct_example: My sister and I walked home.
rules.incorrect_example: My sister and i walked home.

rules.rule: Capitalize first names, last names, and nicknames of specific people and pets.
rules.correct_example: Maya and her dog Biscuit visited Grandpa Joe.
rules.incorrect_example: maya and her dog biscuit visited grandpa joe.

rules.rule: Capitalize the names of months and days of the week.
rules.correct_example: Our trip starts on Monday, June 3.
rules.incorrect_example: Our trip starts on monday, june 3.

rules.rule: Do not capitalize seasons (spring, summer, fall, winter) unless they start a sentence or are part of a proper name.
rules.correct_example: We go camping every summer.
rules.incorrect_example: We go camping every Summer.

rules.rule: Capitalize the names of holidays and special days.
rules.correct_example: We light candles on Diwali and eat turkey on Thanksgiving.
rules.incorrect_example: We light candles on diwali and eat turkey on thanksgiving.

rules.rule: Capitalize the names of specific places: cities, states, countries, rivers, mountains, streets, and parks.
rules.correct_example: We hiked near Lake Tahoe on our way to Nevada.
rules.incorrect_example: We hiked near lake tahoe on our way to nevada.

rules.rule: Capitalize brand and product names, but not the common noun that follows them.
rules.correct_example: She bought Nike shoes and a box of Cheerios.
rules.incorrect_example: She bought nike Shoes and a box of cheerios.

rules.rule: In titles, capitalize the first and last words and all major words. Short articles, conjunctions, and prepositions (a, the, and, of, in) stay lowercase unless they come first or last.
rules.correct_example: My favorite book is *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*.
rules.incorrect_example: My favorite book is *The Lion, The Witch And The Wardrobe*.

style_variants.chicago_mla: Lowercase all prepositions, regardless of length.
style_variants.ap_apa: Capitalize prepositions and conjunctions of four or more letters (e.g., With, From, About).

rules.rule: Capitalize a title used right before a name or as a name (Dr. Patel, Aunt Rosa, 'Thanks, Mom'). Lowercase it when used as a general word (the doctor, my aunt, my mom).
rules.correct_example: I told Mom that my aunt met Principal Lee.
rules.incorrect_example: I told mom that my Aunt met principal Lee.

rules.rule: Capitalize names of organizations, teams, languages, nationalities, and religions.
rules.correct_example: The Girl Scouts invited a Spanish teacher who is Mexican American.
rules.incorrect_example: The girl scouts invited a spanish teacher who is mexican american.

rules.rule: Capitalize the first word of a quoted full sentence. Do not capitalize the second half of a quotation that was interrupted mid-sentence.
rules.correct_example: "After lunch," said Ravi, "we can play outside."
rules.incorrect_example: "After lunch," said Ravi, "We can play outside."

rules.rule: Capitalize compass words when they name a region (the Midwest, the South). Lowercase them when they give a direction (drive north).
rules.correct_example: We drove south to visit cousins in the Southwest.
rules.incorrect_example: We drove South to visit cousins in the southwest.

rules.rule: Use commas to separate three or more single words in a list.
rules.correct_example: We packed apples, crackers, and cheese.
rules.incorrect_example: We packed apples crackers and cheese.

rules.rule: In a list of three or more words or phrases, a comma before the final 'and' or 'or' (the serial or Oxford comma) is optional in many styles, but use it when leaving it out could cause confusion.
rules.correct_example: I thanked my parents, Ms. Ortiz, and Coach Kim.
rules.incorrect_example: I thanked my parents, Ms. Ortiz and Coach Kim. (reads as if Ms. Ortiz and Coach Kim are the parents)

style_variants.ap: No serial comma unless needed for clarity.

rules.rule: Put a comma between the day and the year, and after the year when the sentence continues. No comma is needed with only a month and year.
rules.correct_example: On July 4, 2026, the town held a parade. It rained in March 2025.
rules.incorrect_example: On July 4 2026 the town held a parade. It rained in March, 2025.

rules.rule: Use a comma after the greeting of a friendly letter and after the closing.
rules.correct_example: Dear Grandma, ... Love, Priya
rules.incorrect_example: Dear Grandma ... Love Priya

style_variants.business_letter: A colon is used after a formal greeting (Dear Dr. Smith:).

rules.rule: Put commas between a city and its state or country, and after the state or country when the sentence continues.
rules.correct_example: She moved from Austin, Texas, to Pune, India.
rules.incorrect_example: She moved from Austin Texas to Pune India.

rules.rule: Use a comma to separate a dialogue tag (she said, he asked) from the spoken words.
rules.correct_example: Leo said, "Let's go."
rules.incorrect_example: Leo said "Let's go."

rules.rule: Put a comma before and, but, or, so, yet, for, or nor when it joins two complete sentences (independent clauses).
rules.correct_example: The game ended, but nobody wanted to go home.
rules.incorrect_example: The game ended but nobody wanted to go home.

style_variants.short_clauses: Many guides allow omitting the comma when both clauses are very short (I ran and I won).

rules.rule: Use a comma after an introductory word, phrase, or dependent clause that comes before the main sentence.
rules.correct_example: When the bell rang, everyone rushed outside.
rules.incorrect_example: When the bell rang everyone rushed outside.

style_variants.short_phrases: A comma after a short introductory prepositional phrase (In 2020 we moved) is often optional.

rules.rule: Use a comma to set off yes, no, well, and similar words at the start of a sentence.
rules.correct_example: Yes, I finished my homework.
rules.incorrect_example: Yes I finished my homework.

rules.rule: Use a comma before a short tag question at the end of a sentence.
rules.correct_example: You fed the cat, didn't you?
rules.incorrect_example: You fed the cat didn't you?

rules.rule: Use commas to set off the name of the person being spoken to, wherever it appears in the sentence.
rules.correct_example: Can you help me, Sam? / Sam, can you help me?
rules.incorrect_example: Can you help me Sam?

rules.rule: Use a pair of commas around a word, phrase, or clause that adds extra information but could be removed without changing the main meaning (often a 'which' clause).
rules.correct_example: My bike, which is bright red, has a flat tire.
rules.incorrect_example: My bike which is bright red has a flat tire.

rules.rule: Use commas around a noun phrase that renames the noun next to it when it is extra information.
rules.correct_example: Ms. Chen, our science teacher, built a robot.
rules.incorrect_example: Ms. Chen our science teacher built a robot.

rules.rule: Do not use commas around information that is needed to identify which person or thing you mean (often a 'that' or 'who' clause that narrows the meaning).
rules.correct_example: Students who finish early may read quietly.
rules.incorrect_example: Students, who finish early, may read quietly.

rules.rule: Put a comma between two adjectives that describe a noun equally (you could reverse them or put 'and' between them). Don't use a comma if the adjectives can't be swapped.
rules.correct_example: It was a long, boring movie. She wore an old green sweater.
rules.incorrect_example: It was a long boring movie. She wore an old, green sweater.

rules.rule: Use a comma before a describing phrase at the end of a sentence when it refers back to the subject, and make sure it's clear who or what it describes.
rules.correct_example: Arjun crossed the finish line, grinning from ear to ear.
rules.incorrect_example: Arjun high-fived Ben, grinning from ear to ear. (unclear who is grinning)

rules.rule: Use a comma to set off a contrasting phrase or a sudden shift near the end of a sentence.
rules.correct_example: He was nervous, not scared.
rules.incorrect_example: He was nervous not scared.

rules.rule: Add a comma when a reader might otherwise group the wrong words together.
rules.correct_example: Inside, the room was freezing.
rules.incorrect_example: Inside the room was freezing. (stumbles as 'inside the room')

rules.rule: Use commas to set off a degree or professional title that follows a name.
rules.correct_example: Ana Ruiz, MD, will speak first.
rules.incorrect_example: Ana Ruiz MD will speak first.

style_variants.suffixes: Most current guides drop the comma before Jr. and Sr. (Martin Luther King Jr.).

rules.rule: Do not put a single comma between a subject and its verb, even when the subject is long.
rules.correct_example: The tallest player on our team scored the winning goal.
rules.incorrect_example: The tallest player on our team, scored the winning goal.

rules.rule: Do not put a comma before 'and' when it joins two verbs that share the same subject (the second part is not a complete sentence).
rules.correct_example: We cleaned the kitchen and started dinner.
rules.incorrect_example: We cleaned the kitchen, and started dinner.

rules.rule: Do not put a comma between just two nouns or noun phrases joined by 'and' or 'or'.
rules.correct_example: My brother and his best friend built a treehouse.
rules.incorrect_example: My brother, and his best friend built a treehouse.

rules.rule: When a dependent clause (because..., when..., if...) comes after the main clause, usually leave the comma out. A comma is acceptable for a strong contrast (although, even though).
rules.correct_example: We stayed inside because it was raining.
rules.incorrect_example: We stayed inside, because it was raining.

rules.rule: Put quotation marks around the exact words a person says, and only around those words.
rules.correct_example: "I'm hungry," said Nia.
rules.incorrect_example: "I'm hungry, said Nia."

rules.rule: In American English, periods and commas go inside the closing quotation mark.
rules.correct_example: "It's finally Friday," she said.
rules.incorrect_example: "It's finally Friday", she said.

style_variants.uk: Punctuation goes inside only if it belongs to the quoted material; single quotation marks are common.

rules.rule: Put a question mark or exclamation mark inside the quotation marks if it belongs to the quoted words, and outside if it belongs to the whole sentence.
rules.correct_example: Mom asked, "Did you lock the door?" / Did she really say "no homework"?
rules.incorrect_example: Mom asked, "Did you lock the door"?

rules.rule: When a dialogue tag interrupts one sentence of speech, close and reopen the quotation marks, use commas around the tag, and keep the second part lowercase.
rules.correct_example: "If we hurry," Dev said, "we can catch the bus."
rules.incorrect_example: "If we hurry" Dev said "We can catch the bus."

rules.rule: Start a new paragraph each time a different person begins speaking.
rules.correct_example:
"Ready?" asked Lily.
"Almost," said Omar.
rules.incorrect_example: "Ready?" asked Lily. "Almost," said Omar.

rules.rule: Do not use quotation marks when reporting what someone said without their exact words (often after 'that' or 'if').
rules.correct_example: Coach said that practice was canceled.
rules.incorrect_example: Coach said that "practice was canceled."

rules.rule: Put quotation marks around words copied exactly from a book, article, or other source.
rules.correct_example: The article calls the bridge "an engineering marvel."
rules.incorrect_example: The article calls the bridge an engineering marvel. (copied words with no marks)

rules.rule: Do not put a comma before a quotation that blends into your own sentence (often after 'that', 'as', or 'called').
rules.correct_example: The author argues that "every vote counts."
rules.incorrect_example: The author argues that, "every vote counts."

rules.rule: You can use a colon to introduce a quotation when a complete sentence comes before it.
rules.correct_example: The sign gave one clear warning: "Do not feed the bears."
rules.incorrect_example: The sign said: "Do not feed the bears."

rules.rule: Use single quotation marks for a quotation inside another quotation.
rules.correct_example: "Did you hear him yell 'surprise'?" asked Mia.
rules.incorrect_example: "Did you hear him yell "surprise"?" asked Mia.

rules.rule: Put quotation marks around titles of short works or parts of larger works: songs, poems, short stories, articles, chapters, and episodes.
rules.correct_example: We read the poem "The Road Not Taken" in class.
rules.incorrect_example: We read the poem *The Road Not Taken* in class.

rules.rule: Italicize (or underline when handwriting) titles of long or complete works: books, movies, TV shows, albums, magazines, newspapers, and video games.
rules.correct_example: My class is reading *Charlotte's Web*.
rules.incorrect_example: My class is reading "Charlotte's Web."

style_variants.ap_news: AP style uses quotation marks for most titles instead of italics.

rules.rule: Quotation marks can set off a phrase used in a special or ironic way, or a borrowed saying. Use them sparingly, and never just for emphasis.
rules.correct_example: Around here, being late is just "the way of things."
rules.incorrect_example: We sell "fresh" bread every day. (quotation marks used for emphasis suggest the bread isn't fresh)

style_variants.words_as_words: When referring to a word itself, many guides prefer italics: The word *their* is often misspelled.

rules.rule: End a statement (telling sentence) with a period.
rules.correct_example: The library opens at nine.
rules.incorrect_example: The library opens at nine

rules.rule: End a direct question with a question mark. Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why, how, or a helping verb (is, can, do).
rules.correct_example: Where did you put my backpack?
rules.incorrect_example: Where did you put my backpack.

rules.rule: Use an exclamation mark to show strong feeling, surprise, or urgency. A period is also correct for many of these sentences; the choice changes the tone.
rules.correct_example: Watch out! / We won the championship!
rules.incorrect_example: Watch out. (in a story where someone is about to be hit, the period undersells the urgency)

style_variants.formal_writing: Exclamation marks are used rarely in formal or academic writing.

rules.rule: End a command or request with a period, or with an exclamation mark if it is urgent or forceful.
rules.correct_example: Please close the door. / Stop!
rules.incorrect_example: Please close the door?

style_variants.polite_requests: Requests phrased as questions (Could you close the door?) take a question mark, though a period is accepted in some formal writing.

rules.rule: A sentence that reports a question without asking it directly ends with a period, not a question mark.
rules.correct_example: I wonder whether the store is open.
rules.incorrect_example: I wonder whether the store is open?

rules.rule: Do not join two complete sentences with only a comma. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and/but/so.
rules.correct_example: It started to rain. We went inside.
rules.incorrect_example: It started to rain, we went inside.

rules.rule: Do not run two complete sentences together with no punctuation at all.
rules.correct_example: My dog loves the park. She runs every morning.
rules.incorrect_example: My dog loves the park she runs every morning.

rules.rule: A sentence needs a subject and a verb and must express a complete thought. Attach fragments to a nearby sentence or complete them.
rules.correct_example: We left early because the roads were icy.
rules.incorrect_example: We left early. Because the roads were icy.

style_variants.creative_writing: Fragments are sometimes used on purpose for effect in stories and dialogue.

rules.rule: If a sentence ends with an abbreviation that already has a period, don't add a second period.
rules.correct_example: The meeting starts at 8 a.m.
rules.incorrect_example: The meeting starts at 8 a.m..

rules.rule: Choose end punctuation to match the tone you want: a period sounds calm or firm, an exclamation mark sounds excited or urgent, and a question mark invites a response.
rules.correct_example: "Fine." (cold) vs. "Fine!" (cheerful)

rules.rule: In standard writing, use one end mark. Avoid stacking marks like !!! or ?!
rules.correct_example: That was amazing!
rules.incorrect_example: That was amazing!!!

style_variants.informal_text: Stacked marks are common in casual messages and comics.

rules.rule: Use parentheses for extra information that is less important than the rest of the sentence, such as a quiet aside, a date, or an example.
rules.correct_example: The museum (which is free on Sundays) was packed.
rules.incorrect_example: The museum (which is free on Sundays was packed.

style_variants.choice: Commas, dashes, and parentheses can all set off extra information. Commas are neutral, dashes add emphasis, and parentheses play it down.

rules.rule: If the words in parentheses are part of a larger sentence, the sentence's period goes outside. If the parentheses hold a complete separate sentence, the period goes inside.
rules.correct_example: We left at noon (or a little after). / We left at noon. (It was a little after.)
rules.incorrect_example: We left at noon (or a little after.)

rules.rule: Use a pair of dashes to set off extra information with emphasis in the middle of a sentence. Don't mix a dash with a comma for the same interruption.
rules.correct_example: My cousin — the one who lives in Toronto — is visiting.
rules.incorrect_example: My cousin — the one who lives in Toronto, is visiting.

style_variants.spacing: Chicago/MLA: em dash with no spaces (Toronto—is). AP: spaces around the dash. UK: often a spaced en dash.

rules.rule: Use a dash to show a sudden break, an interruption, or to introduce a dramatic ending to a sentence.
rules.correct_example: I opened the box and found — nothing.
rules.incorrect_example: I opened the box and found - nothing. (hyphen used instead of a dash)

rules.rule: Use an ellipsis (...) to show a trailing-off thought or a hesitant pause, especially in dialogue.
rules.correct_example: "I thought you knew..." she whispered.
rules.incorrect_example: "I thought you knew....." she whispered.

style_variants.spacing: Some guides space the dots (. . .); most digital writing uses three unspaced dots or the single ellipsis character.

rules.rule: Use an ellipsis to show that words were left out of a quotation, without changing its meaning.
rules.correct_example: Original: "The plan, which took months to finish, finally worked." Shortened: "The plan ... finally worked."
rules.incorrect_example: "The plan finally worked." (words removed with no ellipsis)

rules.rule: Use a semicolon to join two closely related complete sentences without a conjunction.
rules.correct_example: The test was hard; everyone studied for days.
rules.incorrect_example: The test was hard; because everyone was tired.

rules.rule: When words like however, therefore, or meanwhile join two complete sentences, put a semicolon before them and a comma after.
rules.correct_example: I studied all night; however, I still felt nervous.
rules.incorrect_example: I studied all night, however, I still felt nervous.

rules.rule: Use semicolons to separate list items that already contain commas.
rules.correct_example: We visited Austin, Texas; Denver, Colorado; and Reno, Nevada.
rules.incorrect_example: We visited Austin, Texas, Denver, Colorado, and Reno, Nevada.

rules.rule: Use a colon after a complete sentence to introduce a list.
rules.correct_example: Bring three things: a pencil, a ruler, and an eraser.
rules.incorrect_example: Bring three things; a pencil, a ruler, and an eraser.

rules.rule: Do not put a colon directly after a verb or preposition (are, include, such as, of). The words before a colon should form a complete sentence.
rules.correct_example: My favorite fruits are mangoes and grapes.
rules.incorrect_example: My favorite fruits are: mangoes and grapes.

rules.rule: Use a colon after a complete sentence to introduce an explanation, example, or answer to what came before.
rules.correct_example: She had one goal: finish the race.
rules.incorrect_example: She had one goal, finish the race.

style_variants.alternative: A dash is also accepted here (She had one goal — finish the race).
style_variants.capitalization: US style capitalizes a full sentence after a colon in some guides (APA, AP); Chicago lowercases it.

rules.rule: Hyphenate two or more words that work together as one adjective before a noun. Usually don't hyphenate them after the noun.
rules.correct_example: She is a well-known author. The author is well known.
rules.incorrect_example: She is a well known author.

rules.rule: Do not use a hyphen after an adverb ending in -ly.
rules.correct_example: It was a freshly baked pie.
rules.incorrect_example: It was a freshly-baked pie.

rules.rule: Hyphenate spelled-out numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine and fractions used as adjectives.
rules.correct_example: Thirty-two students needed a two-thirds majority.
rules.incorrect_example: Thirty two students needed a two thirds majority.

rules.rule: A hyphen (-) joins words. A dash (—) separates parts of a sentence. Don't use a hyphen where a dash belongs.
rules.correct_example: My sister-in-law called — she had big news.
rules.incorrect_example: My sister in law called - she had big news.

style_variants.typing: Two hyphens (--) are often accepted as a typed dash.
style_variants.en_dash: Some guides use an en dash (–) for ranges (pages 4–9).

rules.rule: In a contraction, the apostrophe goes where letters were removed.
rules.correct_example: I can't come because it's raining.
rules.incorrect_example: I ca'nt come because its raining.

rules.rule: To show that one person or thing owns something, add 's.
rules.correct_example: The dog's bowl is empty.
rules.incorrect_example: The dogs bowl is empty.

rules.rule: For a plural noun that ends in -s, add only an apostrophe after the s to show possession.
rules.correct_example: The students' projects are on display.
rules.incorrect_example: The student's projects are on display. (when many students made them)

rules.rule: For a plural noun that doesn't end in -s (children, people, mice), add 's.
rules.correct_example: The children's books are on the bottom shelf.
rules.incorrect_example: The childrens' books are on the bottom shelf.

rules.rule: For a singular noun or name ending in -s, add 's in most styles (James's, the bus's).
rules.correct_example: We went to James's house.
rules.incorrect_example: We went to Jame's house.

style_variants.ap: Add only an apostrophe to proper names ending in s (James').

rules.rule: Do not use an apostrophe to make an ordinary word plural.
rules.correct_example: We sell fresh bananas.
rules.incorrect_example: We sell fresh banana's.

rules.rule: When two people own something together, only the last name gets 's. When they each own their own, both names get 's.
rules.correct_example: Ana and Raj's dog (one shared dog). Ana's and Raj's bikes (separate bikes).
rules.incorrect_example: Ana's and Raj's dog (when they share one dog)

rules.rule: It's means 'it is' or 'it has.' Its (no apostrophe) shows ownership.
rules.correct_example: It's cold, so the cat curled up in its bed.
rules.incorrect_example: Its cold, so the cat curled up in it's bed.

rules.rule: You're means 'you are.' Your shows ownership.
rules.correct_example: You're going to love your new room.
rules.incorrect_example: Your going to love you're new room.

rules.rule: They're means 'they are.' Their shows ownership. There points to a place or starts a sentence (there is, there are).
rules.correct_example: They're leaving their bags over there.
rules.incorrect_example: Their leaving there bags over they're.

rules.rule: Who's means 'who is' or 'who has.' Whose asks or tells who owns something.
rules.correct_example: Who's coming, and whose jacket is this?
rules.incorrect_example: Whose coming, and who's jacket is this?

rules.rule: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: hers, his, its, ours, yours, theirs.
rules.correct_example: Is this umbrella yours or hers?
rules.incorrect_example: Is this umbrella your's or her's?

rules.rule: Use an apostrophe to make single lowercase letters plural so they aren't misread (p's and q's). Capital letters usually don't need one (three As).
rules.correct_example: Mind your p's and q's. She got three As on her report card.
rules.incorrect_example: Mind your ps and qs.

style_variants.chicago_mla: Apostrophe for lowercase letters only (p's, As).
style_variants.ap: Apostrophe for single letters, including capitals (A's).

rules.rule: Make numbers and decades plural without an apostrophe (the 1990s, two 7s). Use an apostrophe only to replace missing digits ('90s).
rules.correct_example: My parents grew up in the '90s, not the 1980s.
rules.incorrect_example: My parents grew up in the 90's, not the 1980's.

style_variants.older_style: Some older or informal styles accept 1990's; most current guides do not.
